questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A researcher is studying an enzyme that catalyzes a key step in glycolysis. When a competitive inhibitor is added, the Vmax remains unchanged but the Km increases from 2 mM to 8 mM. When a non-competitive inhibitor is added separately, the Km remains unchanged but Vmax decreases from 100 nmol/min to 50 nmol/min. A student claims that a mixed inhibitor would decrease BOTH Vmax and increase Km. Which statement BEST explains the clinical relevance of competitive inhibition in pharmacology?

options.A: Competitive inhibition is irreversible and cannot be overcome by increasing substrate concentration
options.B: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and can be displaced by high substrate concentrations, explaining the rationale for high-dose folinic acid rescue after methotrexate therapy
options.C: Non-competitive inhibition is always more potent than competitive inhibition because it cannot be overcome
options.D: Mixed inhibitors are preferred in drug design because they lower both Km and Vmax simultaneously

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Competitive inhibitors structurally resemble the substrate and bind reversibly to the active site. Because the inhibition is reversible, high substrate concentrations can displace the inhibitor — this is the basis of leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue after methotrexate therapy. Methotrexate competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR); folinic acid bypasses the block by providing pre-formed tetrahydrofolate. Option A is wrong — competitive inhibition is reversible, not irreversible (irreversible inhibition is seen with suicide inhibitors like aspirin on COX). Option C is partially true (non-competitive cannot be overcome by substrate) but clinically less applicable as a standalone statement. Option D is incorrect — mixed inhibitors do raise Km and lower Vmax, but this is not a pharmacological advantage per se. Exam pearl: In competitive inhibition: Km increases, Vmax unchanged. In non-competitive: Vmax decreases, Km unchanged. In uncompetitive: both Km and Vmax decrease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 3-day-old neonate presents with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and hypoglycemia. Blood glucose is 38 mg/dL despite IV dextrose. Urine reducing substances are positive but glucose oxidase test is negative. Liver biopsy shows hepatocyte vacuolation and cirrhosis. Enzyme assay reveals absent galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase activity. Which metabolite accumulation is MOST responsible for the cataract formation in this condition?

options.A: Galactose-1-phosphate
options.B: UDP-galactose
options.C: Galactitol
options.D: Galactonate

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C — Galactitol. This is classic Galactosemia Type I (GALT deficiency). When galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase is absent, galactose accumulates and is shunted via aldose reductase to galactitol. Galactitol accumulates in the lens (it cannot be further metabolized), drawing in water osmotically and causing cataract. Galactose-1-phosphate (option A) is responsible for hepatocyte injury, brain damage, and E. coli sepsis susceptibility — NOT cataracts. UDP-galactose (option B) is not the toxic metabolite. Galactonate (option D) is a minor oxidation product with no significant pathological role. Exam pearl: Galactitol → cataracts; Galactose-1-phosphate → liver, brain, kidney damage. The positive urine reducing substance with negative glucose oxidase test is a classic exam clue pointing to galactosuria (galactose is a reducing sugar but not detected by glucose-specific oxidase strips). Neonates with galactosemia are at high risk for Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis — a commonly tested association.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency room after a 12-hour fast following a viral illness. She is lethargic, hypoglycemic (blood glucose 28 mg/dL), and has no ketonemia. Urine acylcarnitine profile shows elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8) and decanoylcarnitine (C10). Plasma free carnitine is low. Which enzyme deficiency BEST explains this presentation?

options.A: Long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCAD)
options.B: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD)
options.C: Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD)
options.D: Very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (VLCAD)

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — MCAD deficiency. This is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder. MCAD deficiency presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting or illness, typically in infants 3–24 months. The hallmark is elevated C8 (octanoylcarnitine) and C10 (decanoylcarnitine) on acylcarnitine profile — medium-chain fatty acids accumulate because they cannot be oxidized. No ketones are produced because acetyl-CoA is not generated. LCAD (option A) would show different acylcarnitine profile (C14 elevation). SCAD (option C) shows C4 (butyrylcarnitine) elevation — usually milder phenotype. VLCAD (option D) shows C14:1 elevation with cardiomyopathy as a feature. Exam pearl: MCAD is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder; screened on newborn metabolic screening (tandem MS). Classic triad: hypoketotic hypoglycemia + fasting intolerance + elevated C8 acylcarnitine. Can present as sudden infant death (SIDS). Urine organic acids show dicarboxylic aciduria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 2-day-old male neonate develops poor feeding, vomiting, and progressive encephalopathy. Serum ammonia is 850 µmol/L (normal <100). Blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis. Plasma amino acid analysis reveals elevated citrulline (800 µmol/L, normal <30) and argininosuccinate. Urine orotic acid is markedly elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?

options.A: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I)
options.B: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC)
options.C: Argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS)
options.D: Argininosuccinate lyase (ASL)

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C — Argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) deficiency = Citrullinemia Type I. The key distinguishing feature is markedly elevated citrulline (>1000 µmol/L). Citrulline accumulates because it cannot be converted to argininosuccinate. The elevated urine orotic acid differentiates this from CPS-I deficiency (where orotic acid is LOW/normal because carbamoyl phosphate doesn't accumulate to spill into pyrimidine synthesis). In OTC deficiency (option B): citrulline is low/normal, orotic acid is very high, and it is X-linked. In ASL deficiency (option D): argininosuccinate accumulates, not citrulline. CPS-I (option A): citrulline is very low, orotic acid is normal/low. Exam pearl: Urine orotic acid is the key discriminator: HIGH in OTC and ASS deficiencies; LOW/NORMAL in CPS-I and NAGS deficiency. Citrulline levels: Very high → ASS deficiency; Moderate elevation → OTC; Low/absent → CPS-I or NAGS.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old alcoholic male presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. He also has peripheral neuropathy and glossitis. IV thiamine is administered with partial improvement. Which coenzyme form of thiamine is essential for the enzyme most directly impaired in his encephalopathy?

options.A: Thiamine monophosphate (TMP)
options.B: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)
options.C: Thiamine triphosphate (TTP)
options.D: Free thiamine

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), also called thiamine diphosphate. TPP is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1. In Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency), the most critically impaired enzyme is pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) which requires TPP. Without TPP, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and accumulates — leading to lactic acidosis. Other TPP-dependent enzymes: alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (TCA cycle), branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCAADH — impaired in maple syrup urine disease), and transketolase (pentose phosphate pathway — used as the most sensitive marker of thiamine deficiency). TMP (option A) is a storage form. TTP (option C) has a role in nerve conduction but is not the primary coenzyme. Free thiamine (option D) is inactive. Exam pearl: TPP-dependent enzymes mnemonic — 'Pyruvate Dehydrogenase, Alpha-Ketoglutarate, Branched-chain keto acid DH, Transketolase' (PABT). Transketolase assay in RBCs is the most sensitive test for thiamine deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A research team is studying a bacterial mutant that cannot replicate its chromosome. They find that in this mutant, newly synthesized short DNA fragments accumulate and are never joined into a continuous strand on one template strand, but replication on the other template strand proceeds normally. Which enzyme is MOST likely deficient in this mutant?

options.A: DNA Polymerase III
options.B: DNA Primase
options.C: DNA Ligase
options.D: DNA Helicase

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C — DNA Ligase. The question describes the accumulation of Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand. During replication, the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments (each initiated by a primer). After RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA by DNA Pol I (in prokaryotes), DNA ligase seals the nicks between fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds. If DNA ligase is absent, Okazaki fragments cannot be joined, exactly as described. DNA Pol III (option A) is the main replicative polymerase — its absence would halt synthesis entirely. DNA Primase (option B) synthesizes the RNA primer; its absence would prevent initiation of Okazaki fragments, not their joining. DNA Helicase (option D) unwinds the double helix; its absence would halt the entire replication fork. Exam pearl: Okazaki fragments are 1000–2000 nt in prokaryotes and 100–200 nt in eukaryotes. The enzyme that joins them is DNA ligase (requires NAD+ in prokaryotes, ATP in eukaryotes). Clinically: DNA ligase deficiency → Bloom syndrome (increased chromosome breakage, predisposition to cancer, short stature).

P50 value (partial pressure at 50% saturation) normally ~26 mmHg
Right shift: increased 2,3-BPG, acidosis, hyperthermia, hypercapnia
Left shift: fetal hemoglobin (HbF), carboxyhemoglobin, alkalosis, hypothermia
Bohr effect: CO2 and H+ cause right shift in tissues
Effect of 2,3-BPG on oxygen release to tissues
questions.question_text: Referring to the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shown, a patient is admitted after carbon monoxide poisoning. Pulse oximetry reads 99% SpO2 but the patient is cyanotic and confused. Blood co-oximetry reveals HbCO of 35%. Which shift in the dissociation curve and which mechanism BEST explains the tissue hypoxia?

options.A: Right shift due to increased 2,3-BPG, reducing oxygen affinity and impairing tissue delivery
options.B: Left shift due to carboxyhemoglobin, increasing oxygen affinity and impairing oxygen unloading to tissues
options.C: No shift; tissue hypoxia is due solely to reduced hemoglobin available for oxygen transport
options.D: Right shift due to metabolic acidosis from tissue hypoxia, which is protective in CO poisoning

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with ~240× the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin (HbCO). This has TWO effects: (1) It reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity by occupying Hb binding sites. (2) More importantly, HbCO causes a LEFT SHIFT of the ODC — the remaining oxygenated Hb cannot unload O2 to tissues (Haldane effect). Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from HbCO, falsely showing high SpO2 — hence the 'normal' reading despite toxicity. Co-oximetry (which measures multiple Hb species at different wavelengths) is needed for diagnosis. Option A is wrong — 2,3-BPG causes a right shift; CO causes left shift. Option C is incomplete — the left shift (impaired unloading) is the primary killing mechanism, not just reduced capacity. Option D is wrong — any right shift would actually be a compensatory response but is not the primary mechanism. Exam pearl: CO poisoning ODC left shift = Haldane effect. Cyanide poisoning also causes histotoxic hypoxia but via cytochrome c oxidase inhibition. Treatment: 100% O2 (competitive displacement of CO), hyperbaric O2 in severe cases.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: An investigator labels acetyl-CoA with 14C at C1 and C2 (both carbons of the acetyl group) and tracks the label through one complete turn of the TCA cycle. After one complete turn of the cycle, in which product will the 14C label be PREDOMINANTLY found?

options.A: Oxaloacetate (both carbons lost as CO2)
options.B: CO2 released at isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase steps
options.C: Succinate, fumarate, and malate (the label is retained in the 4-carbon backbone)
options.D: Citrate (the label is diluted but retained in the first condensation product)

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. This is a classic carbon tracking question. When labeled acetyl-CoA (C1, C2) condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate, the two carbons of acetyl-CoA become C1 and C2 of citrate (or equivalently, the C5 and C6 carbons, depending on numbering). The two CO2 molecules released (at isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) come from the OXALOACETATE carbons (C1 and C4 of oxaloacetate), NOT from the acetyl-CoA carbons — in the FIRST turn of the cycle. Therefore, the acetyl-CoA label is retained in the 4-carbon intermediates: succinate, fumarate, malate, and regenerated oxaloacetate. The label exits as CO2 only in the SECOND turn of the cycle. Option A is incorrect — OAA carbons are lost as CO2 in the first turn, not the acetyl carbons. Option B is incorrect for the same reason. Option D is partially true (label is in citrate) but citrate is converted through the cycle. Exam pearl: 'In the first turn of TCA, the acetyl carbons are NOT lost as CO2 — they are retained in the 4-carbon intermediates.' This is a frequently tested and frequently missed concept.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man with familial hypercholesterolemia is started on atorvastatin. His LDL falls from 320 mg/dL to 180 mg/dL after 3 months. The mechanism by which statins lower LDL involves inhibition of which enzyme and what downstream compensatory change?

options.A: Inhibition of squalene epoxidase → decreased LDL receptor expression
options.B: Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase → increased LDL receptor upregulation in hepatocytes
options.C: Inhibition of HMG-CoA synthase → decreased VLDL production by the liver
options.D: Inhibition of PCSK9 → increased LDL receptor degradation

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the mevalonate pathway (cholesterol synthesis). This reduces intracellular cholesterol in hepatocytes. As a compensatory response, hepatocytes upregulate LDL receptors on their surface to capture more LDL-cholesterol from the bloodstream — this is the PRIMARY mechanism by which LDL levels fall. Option A: Squalene epoxidase is inhibited by terbinafine (antifungal), not statins. Option C: HMG-CoA synthase is not the target; HMG-CoA reductase is. Option D: PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) prevent LDL receptor degradation — this is a different drug class, not statins. Exam pearl: Statin mechanism = HMG-CoA reductase inhibition → ↓ intrahepatic cholesterol → ↑ SREBP-2 activation → ↑ LDL receptor transcription → ↑ LDL uptake from plasma. Side effects: myopathy (rhabdomyolysis in severe cases), hepatotoxicity. Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic via mevalonate pathway inhibition affecting fetal development).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A geneticist studies a mutation that converts a codon from GAG (Glutamic acid) to GUG in the beta-globin mRNA. The resulting protein has valine instead of glutamic acid at position 6. This results in HbS. A second patient has a mutation that converts UAU (Tyrosine) to UAA. What type of mutation is the second and what is its consequence?

options.A: Missense mutation; results in conservative amino acid substitution with mild phenotype
options.B: Nonsense mutation; introduces a premature stop codon, producing a truncated, non-functional protein
options.C: Silent mutation; no change in amino acid, no effect on protein function
options.D: Frameshift mutation; shifts the reading frame, producing a completely altered downstream sequence

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. UAU codes for Tyrosine. UAA is one of the three stop codons (UAA = ochre, UAG = amber, UGA = opal). This is a nonsense mutation — a point mutation that converts a sense codon to a stop codon, resulting in premature termination of translation and a truncated, typically non-functional protein. The first mutation described (GAG→GUG, Glu→Val) is a classic missense mutation — seen in sickle cell disease (HbS). The second mutation (UAU→UAA) is a nonsense mutation. Option A: Missense mutations produce amino acid changes; conservative if similar residue, non-conservative if different class. This question's second mutation is NOT missense. Option C: Silent mutations change the codon but not the amino acid (due to degeneracy of genetic code). Option D: Frameshift mutations occur due to insertions or deletions of nucleotides not in multiples of 3. Exam pearl: Nonsense mutations → NMD (nonsense-mediated mRNA decay) — the aberrant mRNA is degraded. Seen in beta-thalassemia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Three stop codons: UAA (ochre), UAG (amber), UGA (opal).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 5-year-old boy presents with hepatomegaly, recurrent fasting hypoglycemia, and marked elevation of plasma triglycerides and cholesterol. Liver biopsy shows massive glycogen accumulation with normal glycogen structure. Enzyme assay shows absent glucose-6-phosphatase activity. Which metabolic consequence directly explains the hypertriglyceridemia?

options.A: Decreased VLDL synthesis due to hepatic steatosis
options.B: Excess glucose-6-phosphate is shunted into de novo lipogenesis via acetyl-CoA, producing excess triglycerides
options.C: Increased fatty acid oxidation produces excess acetyl-CoA that is converted to cholesterol
options.D: Impaired LDL receptor function due to hepatic glycogen accumulation

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. This is Von Gierke disease (GSD Type Ia) — glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. Without G6Pase, glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose for export. It accumulates and is shunted into: (1) Glycolysis → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → de novo lipogenesis → triglycerides (explaining hypertriglyceridemia and hepatic steatosis). (2) Pentose phosphate pathway → excess NADPH further drives fatty acid synthesis. (3) Glycogen synthesis → hepatomegaly. The elevated triglycerides also result in secondary hypercholesterolemia. Option A: VLDL synthesis is actually INCREASED (not decreased) due to excess lipid substrate. Option C: Fatty acid OXIDATION is decreased in GSD Ia (excess substrate drives synthesis, not oxidation). Option D: LDL receptor impairment is not a feature of GSD. Exam pearl: Von Gierke disease triad: hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia + hyperlipidemia. Also causes hyperuricemia (gout) due to increased uric acid production from excess G6P via pentose phosphate pathway. Lactic acidosis due to excess pyruvate. Kidney involvement (nephromegaly) is also seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 12-year-old boy presents with recurrent joint dislocations, hyperextensible skin, and easy bruising. His wounds heal poorly. Serum lysyl oxidase is markedly reduced. Urine shows elevated hydroxylysine-containing peptides. Which post-translational modification is MOST impaired in this patient's collagen?

options.A: Prolyl hydroxylation requiring vitamin C
options.B: Cross-linking of lysine residues between collagen fibrils
options.C: Signal peptide cleavage during entry into the ER
options.D: N-glycosylation of asparagine residues

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Lysyl oxidase is the enzyme responsible for oxidative deamination of lysine (and hydroxylysine) residues in collagen and elastin, forming allysine. These aldehyde groups then spontaneously condense to form covalent cross-links between collagen fibrils and between elastin molecules, providing tensile strength and resistance to mechanical stress. Deficiency of lysyl oxidase causes Menkes disease (X-linked, copper deficiency) and is also impaired in copper deficiency since lysyl oxidase requires copper as a cofactor. The presentation here mimics Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) — joint hypermobility, skin extensibility, poor wound healing. Option A: Prolyl hydroxylation requires vitamin C; its impairment causes scurvy (not the primary issue here — lysyl oxidase is specifically mentioned). Option C: Signal peptide cleavage is a cotranslational event, not a collagen-specific modification impaired here. Option D: Collagen undergoes O-glycosylation (not N-glycosylation) at hydroxylysine residues. Exam pearl: Lysyl oxidase requires copper. Menkes disease = X-linked copper deficiency → ↓ lysyl oxidase → fragile collagen/elastin. EDS Type VI = lysyl hydroxylase deficiency (different enzyme, requires vitamin C).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old type 1 diabetic presents with nausea, vomiting, fruity breath, and deep sighing respirations (Kussmaul breathing). Blood gas: pH 7.1, HCO3 8 mEq/L, glucose 480 mg/dL. Urine ketones strongly positive. Which enzyme is PRIMARILY responsible for the accelerated ketogenesis in this patient, and where does it function?

options.A: HMG-CoA synthase in the cytoplasm
options.B: HMG-CoA lyase in the mitochondrial matrix
options.C: Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase in the cytoplasm
options.D: Succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate-CoA transferase (thiophorase) in the mitochondria

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — HMG-CoA lyase in the mitochondrial matrix. Ketogenesis occurs exclusively in hepatic mitochondria. The pathway: Acetyl-CoA → Acetoacetyl-CoA (thiolase) → HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase, mitochondrial isoform) → Acetoacetate + Acetyl-CoA (HMG-CoA lyase). The rate-limiting step is HMG-CoA lyase, which cleaves HMG-CoA to produce acetoacetate. In DKA, absent insulin → ↑ glucagon → ↑ lipolysis → excess fatty acids → excess acetyl-CoA → overwhelmed TCA cycle → ketogenesis. Option A: HMG-CoA synthase has two isoforms — mitochondrial (ketogenesis) and cytoplasmic (cholesterol synthesis). The cytoplasmic form is not involved in ketone body production. Option C: Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase is an earlier step; not the rate-limiting or primary regulatory step. Option D: Thiophorase is the KEY enzyme in KETONE BODY UTILIZATION (in extrahepatic tissues) — the liver lacks this enzyme, which is why the liver cannot use its own ketone bodies. Exam pearl: Liver produces but cannot use ketones (no thiophorase). Brain, muscle, heart can use ketones. In starvation, brain shifts from glucose to ketone utilization after 3–4 days.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with intellectual disability, choreoathetosis, self-mutilating behavior (lip biting), and hyperuricemia. Serum uric acid is 12 mg/dL. His urine shows an orange sandy precipitate. Enzyme assay shows near-zero HGPRT activity. Which metabolic consequence directly causes the hyperuricemia?

options.A: Increased de novo purine synthesis due to accumulation of PRPP
options.B: Decreased purine degradation due to xanthine oxidase inhibition
options.C: Increased conversion of adenosine to inosine by adenosine deaminase
options.D: Decreased uric acid excretion by the kidneys due to renal tubular dysfunction

questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. This is Lesch-Nyhan syndrome — X-linked deficiency of HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase). Normally, HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine and guanine back to IMP and GMP using PRPP. Without HGPRT: (1) Hypoxanthine and guanine are not salvaged and instead are degraded all the way to uric acid — causing hyperuricemia. (2) PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate) accumulates since it's not consumed by the salvage pathway. Excess PRPP drives de novo purine synthesis (PRPP is the committed substrate), further generating purines that ultimately become uric acid. Option B: Xanthine oxidase is the enzyme that MAKES uric acid; inhibiting it (allopurinol mechanism) would LOWER uric acid. Option C: Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine to inosine — its excess activity occurs in SCID context, not Lesch-Nyhan. Option D: Renal excretion is not primarily impaired; the problem is overproduction. Exam pearl: Treatment of Lesch-Nyhan — allopurinol for hyperuricemia (inhibits xanthine oxidase) but does NOT treat the neurological features. Self-mutilation is the pathognomonic feature. HGPRT gene on X chromosome (Xq26) → only males affected.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 6-month-old exclusively breastfed infant from a northern city (minimal sunlight exposure) presents with bowing of legs, hypocalcemia, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase. Skull X-ray shows craniotabes. Which biochemical profile is MOST consistent with nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets at this stage?

options.A: Low calcium, low phosphorus, low PTH, high alkaline phosphatase
options.B: Low calcium, low phosphorus, high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), high alkaline phosphatase
options.C: Normal calcium, low phosphorus, normal PTH, high alkaline phosphatase
options.D: Low calcium, high phosphorus, low PTH, normal alkaline phosphatase

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. In vitamin D deficiency rickets: (1) Low 1,25-(OH)2 D3 → decreased intestinal Ca and P absorption → hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia. (2) Hypocalcemia stimulates PTH secretion → secondary hyperparathyroidism. PTH then: mobilizes Ca from bone, increases renal Ca reabsorption, decreases renal P reabsorption (causing further phosphaturia → hypophosphatemia), and stimulates 1-alpha hydroxylase. (3) High alkaline phosphatase reflects increased osteoblastic activity trying to mineralize uncalcified osteoid. Option A: Low PTH would suggest hypoparathyroidism, not the expected response. Option C: Hypophosphatemic rickets (X-linked) shows normal calcium but low phosphorus — the profile differs. Option D: High phosphorus with low calcium suggests hypoparathyroidism. Exam pearl: Key differences — Nutritional rickets: ↓Ca, ↓P, ↑PTH, ↑ALP, ↓25(OH)D. X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (FGF23 excess): normal Ca, ↓P, normal/high PTH, ↑ALP, normal 25(OH)D but ↓1,25(OH)2D. Vitamin D-dependent rickets Type II (VDR mutation): high 1,25(OH)2D but resistance.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A newborn girl is noted to be fair-skinned with blue eyes and blonde hair, while both parents are dark-complexioned. At 4 months, she develops seizures and eczema. Her blood phenylalanine is 28 mg/dL (normal <2 mg/dL). Urine has a mousy/musty odor. Newborn metabolic screening had flagged an abnormal result. Which treatment modification is MOST important to prevent intellectual disability in this child?

options.A: Restrict all protein intake severely from birth
options.B: Initiate a phenylalanine-restricted, tyrosine-supplemented diet immediately
options.C: Administer tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) supplementation as first-line therapy for all cases
options.D: Restrict aromatic amino acids and supplement with branched-chain amino acids

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. This is classic Phenylketonuria (PKU) — autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). Phenylalanine accumulates (cannot be converted to tyrosine) and is shunted to phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate (causing mousy odor), and phenyllactate. Accumulated phenylalanine is neurotoxic — interfering with brain development and myelination. Treatment: Phenylalanine-restricted diet (avoiding high-protein foods) PLUS tyrosine supplementation (since tyrosine becomes essential in PKU — it cannot be synthesized from Phe). Option A: Severely restricting ALL protein would cause protein malnutrition; careful Phe restriction with adequate other amino acids is needed. Option C: BH4 (sapropterin) is used for BH4-responsive PKU and BH4 deficiency (which causes a more severe phenotype with neurotransmitter deficiency) — not all PKU cases respond. It's a second-line/adjunct treatment, not first-line for all. Option D: Aromatic amino acid restriction is the principle, but supplementing branched-chain amino acids is not the key intervention — tyrosine supplementation is. Exam pearl: PKU screened by Guthrie test (bacterial inhibition assay) or tandem MS. Maternal PKU (untreated pregnant woman with PKU) → teratogenic to fetus: microcephaly, CHD, growth restriction — even if fetus is heterozygous.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old African-American soldier develops hemolytic anemia after being given primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Blood smear shows Heinz bodies. He recovers spontaneously after stopping the drug. His brother has the same condition. Genetic analysis shows a G6PD variant with markedly reduced stability in older red cells but near-normal activity in reticulocytes. Which biochemical mechanism underlies the RBC destruction?

options.A: Reduced NADPH → inadequate glutathione reduction → oxidative damage to RBC membranes and hemoglobin
options.B: Reduced NADH → impaired electron transport chain in RBCs → ATP depletion
options.C: Excess NADPH production → membrane lipid peroxidation
options.D: Reduced ribose-5-phosphate → impaired nucleotide synthesis in RBCs

questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. G6PD (Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) is the first enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). It generates NADPH from NADP+. NADPH is essential for: (1) Maintaining glutathione in the reduced form (GSH) via glutathione reductase. (2) GSH protects RBC proteins and membranes from oxidative damage via glutathione peroxidase. In G6PD deficiency, oxidative stress (from drugs like primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin; foods like fava beans; infections) cannot be neutralized → hemoglobin is oxidized → Heinz bodies (precipitated denatured Hb) → RBC destruction. Option B: RBCs are anucleate and lack mitochondria — they have no ETC or NADH-dependent ATP production. Their only ATP source is glycolysis. Option C: Excess NADPH would be protective, not harmful. Option D: Ribose-5-phosphate reduction would impair nucleotide synthesis but RBCs don't synthesize nucleotides. Exam pearl: G6PD is most common human enzyme deficiency (X-linked recessive). African type (A-) has 10% residual activity in mature RBCs but near-normal in reticulocytes — so hemolysis is self-limited (young RBCs survive). Mediterranean type is more severe with very low G6PD in all cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A molecular biology researcher finds that a certain proto-oncogene is normally transcribed at low levels. However, a chromosomal translocation places this gene adjacent to an immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer, resulting in constitutive overexpression. The protein product normally regulates the G1 to S phase transition of the cell cycle. Which cancer-causing gene and mechanism does this BEST describe?

options.A: BCR-ABL fusion → constitutively active tyrosine kinase → CML
options.B: MYC translocation t(8;14) → transcriptional activation of cell cycle genes → Burkitt lymphoma
options.C: RB1 deletion → loss of G1/S checkpoint → retinoblastoma
options.D: KRAS point mutation → constitutively active GTPase → colorectal cancer

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — MYC translocation in Burkitt lymphoma. The question describes: (1) Proto-oncogene placed near an immunoglobulin enhancer → constitutive overexpression (this is the Ig heavy chain enhancer at chromosome 14q32). (2) The gene product regulates G1→S transition. MYC (c-Myc) is a transcription factor that drives expression of cyclin D, CDK4, and other cell cycle genes promoting G1→S transition. Translocation t(8;14) places c-MYC (8q24) next to IgH enhancer (14q32) → overexpression → uncontrolled proliferation → Burkitt lymphoma. Option A: BCR-ABL is a fusion gene (not enhancer-driven overexpression) producing constitutive tyrosine kinase — CML. Option C: RB1 is a tumor suppressor (loss of function) — not a proto-oncogene activated by translocation. Option D: KRAS point mutation (Gly12Val) causes constitutive GTP binding — not translocation/enhancer mechanism. Exam pearl: Burkitt lymphoma translocations: t(8;14) most common (80%), t(8;22), t(2;8). Associated with EBV in endemic African type. Starry sky appearance on histology (macrophages engulfing apoptotic tumor cells).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A patient with alcohol-induced liver disease presents with profound hypoglycemia after a 24-hour drinking binge with no food intake. The mechanism of alcohol-induced hypoglycemia involves inhibition of gluconeogenesis. Which specific step in gluconeogenesis is MOST impaired by the elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio caused by alcohol metabolism?

options.A: Conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase
options.B: Conversion of oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate by PEPCK
options.C: Conversion of lactate to pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase
options.D: Conversion of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate by FBPase-1

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. Alcohol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), both of which use NAD+ as cofactor and produce NADH. This massively elevates the NADH/NAD+ ratio. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) equilibrium: Pyruvate + NADH ⇌ Lactate + NAD+. When NADH is elevated, this equilibrium is driven to the RIGHT → lactate accumulates, pyruvate is depleted. Since pyruvate is the primary gluconeogenic precursor, its depletion halts gluconeogenesis. Additionally, the high NADH/NAD+ ratio also converts oxaloacetate to malate (malate dehydrogenase equilibrium shifts), depleting OAA and further impairing gluconeogenesis. Option A: Pyruvate carboxylase is not directly inhibited by NADH ratio — it requires biotin and acetyl-CoA. Option B: PEPCK converts OAA to PEP — this step is impaired secondarily (due to OAA depletion) but the PRIMARY impairment is lactate/pyruvate. Option D: FBPase-1 is a later gluconeogenic step not primarily affected by NADH. Exam pearl: Alcohol causes lactic acidosis (elevated lactate) + hypoglycemia + hyperuricemia (lactate competes with urate for renal excretion). NADH/NAD+ ratio = key concept in alcohol metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman with recurrent pancreatitis has serum triglycerides of 4200 mg/dL. Her serum is lactescent (milky). She has eruptive xanthomas. Genetic testing reveals absent lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity. Which lipoprotein would be MOST elevated, and what is the primary role of its missing activator?

options.A: LDL elevated; LPL normally activated by apoB-100 to hydrolyze LDL-cholesterol
options.B: VLDL elevated; LPL normally activated by apoC-II to hydrolyze VLDL and chylomicron triglycerides
options.C: Chylomicrons elevated; LPL normally activated by apoE to deliver cholesterol to the liver
options.D: HDL elevated; LPL normally activated by apoA-I to promote reverse cholesterol transport

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. LPL deficiency (Fredrickson Type I hyperlipoproteinemia) leads to failure to hydrolyze triglycerides in chylomicrons AND VLDL. Both accumulate. The question asks what is most elevated — in Type I, chylomicrons are massively elevated. However, the key teaching point here is the activator: LPL is activated by apoC-II (present on chylomicrons and VLDL). ApoC-II deficiency has the same phenotype as LPL deficiency. LPL hydrolyzes the triglyceride core of chylomicrons and VLDL in capillaries of adipose tissue and muscle. Option A: ApoB-100 is the ligand for LDL receptor, not an LPL activator. Option C: ApoE is a ligand for hepatic lipoprotein receptors — it facilitates remnant clearance, not LPL activation. Option D: ApoA-I activates LCAT (not LPL) in reverse cholesterol transport. Exam pearl: LPL activator = apoC-II. LPL inhibitor = apoC-III. LPL deficiency → chylomicronemia → pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis. HDL is LOW in LPL deficiency (because HDL acquires surface components from chylomicron hydrolysis). Treatment: severely fat-restricted diet; gene therapy (alipogene tiparvovec — first approved gene therapy in Europe).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 14-year-old boy presents with downward lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), intellectual disability, Marfanoid habitus, and a history of stroke. Urinary nitroprusside test is positive. Serum homocysteine is markedly elevated. Methionine levels are also elevated. Which enzyme deficiency is MOST likely responsible for this presentation?

options.A: Methionine synthase (uses vitamin B12 as cofactor)
options.B: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR)
options.C: Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) requiring pyridoxal phosphate
options.D: Cystathionine gamma-lyase

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C — Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency = Classic homocystinuria. In the transsulfuration pathway: Homocysteine + Serine → Cystathionine (catalyzed by CBS, requires PLP/B6). If CBS is deficient: Homocysteine cannot be converted to cystathionine → homocysteine and methionine accumulate. Homocysteine is thrombogenic (damages vascular endothelium) → stroke and thromboembolism at young age. Ectopia lentis is DOWNWARD in homocystinuria (vs. UPWARD in Marfan syndrome). Option A: Methionine synthase deficiency (B12-dependent) would cause hyperhomocysteinemia but NORMAL or LOW methionine (because Hcy cannot be remethylated back to methionine). Option B: MTHFR deficiency causes mild hyperhomocysteinemia with normal methionine — not the severe phenotype described. Option D: Cystathionine gamma-lyase converts cystathionine to cysteine; its deficiency causes cystathioninuria (benign). Exam pearl: Homocystinuria — mental retardation, Marfanoid features, ectopia lentis (downward), thrombosis. CBS requires B6 (PLP). ~50% of cases respond to high-dose B6 therapy. B12 and folate reduce Hcy by facilitating remethylation. Urine nitroprusside (cyanide-nitroprusside) test is positive for homocysteine AND cystine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A child is born with multiple anomalies. Genetic analysis reveals a deletion on the maternally derived chromosome 15 (del 15q11-q13). The father's chromosome 15 is normal but the paternal allele at this locus is silenced by methylation. Which term describes this mechanism, and what syndrome results?

options.A: X-inactivation; Turner syndrome
options.B: Genomic imprinting; Angelman syndrome
options.C: Genomic imprinting; Prader-Willi syndrome
options.D: Gene amplification; Angelman syndrome

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Genomic imprinting causing Angelman syndrome. Genomic imprinting is a form of epigenetic regulation where certain genes are expressed only from one parental allele due to differential methylation. At chromosome 15q11-q13: The UBE3A gene (encoding E3 ubiquitin ligase) is expressed ONLY from the MATERNAL allele in neurons (paternal allele is silenced by imprinting). If the MATERNAL allele is deleted → no UBE3A expression → Angelman syndrome (happy puppet syndrome): intellectual disability, seizures, inappropriate laughter, absent speech, ataxic gait. If the PATERNAL allele is deleted (or there is maternal uniparental disomy) → Prader-Willi syndrome: hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, short stature, hypogonadism. Option A: X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis) is a different mechanism; Turner syndrome is due to 45,X karyotype. Option C: Prader-Willi requires PATERNAL deletion (not maternal). Option D: Gene amplification is a cancer mechanism (e.g., MYCN in neuroblastoma). Exam pearl: Angelman = maternal deletion 15q11 (or paternal UPD, or UBE3A mutation). Prader-Willi = paternal deletion 15q11 (or maternal UPD). Both involve imprinting at the same chromosomal locus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A patient develops a progressive neurodegenerative disease with memory loss and personality changes. Brain biopsy shows accumulation of abnormal, protease-resistant prion protein (PrPSc) without any viral nucleic acid. The normal prion protein (PrPC) and PrPSc have identical primary sequences but different conformations. Which concept in protein biochemistry does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: Post-translational glycosylation determines protein function
options.B: Protein function is determined by primary sequence alone
options.C: The same primary sequence can fold into different conformations with distinct functions — secondary/tertiary structure determines function
options.D: Prions are examples of non-coding RNA-mediated disease

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. Prion diseases (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, kuru, scrapie, BSE) are the paradigmatic example that identical primary sequences can adopt different conformations with profoundly different properties. PrPC (normal): alpha-helix rich, soluble, sensitive to proteinase K digestion. PrPSc (pathological): beta-sheet rich, insoluble, protease-resistant, infectious. The conversion is autocatalytic: PrPSc acts as a template to convert PrPC to PrPSc. This demonstrates that secondary and tertiary structure — not primary sequence alone — determine protein function. Option A: Glycosylation differences between PrPC and PrPSc are not the primary distinguishing feature. Option B: This is the incorrect 'Anfinsen dogma' oversimplification — Anfinsen showed that primary sequence determines native fold under normal conditions, but prions prove that alternative, stable, pathological folds can exist. Option D: Prions have no nucleic acid component — this is what makes them unique infectious agents (violating Koch's postulates and the central dogma of infectivity). Exam pearl: Prions = proteinaceous infectious particles. No DNA, RNA, lipid, or carbohydrate required for infectivity. Heat-resistant, radiation-resistant. PrP gene (PRNP) is on chromosome 20 in humans.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 4-month-old infant develops vomiting, hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly when fruits and juices are introduced into the diet. Reducing substances are positive in urine. Liver function tests show elevated transaminases. The condition is caused by a deficiency in which enzyme, and what is the metabolite responsible for toxicity?

options.A: Fructokinase; fructose accumulation causes osmotic cataracts
options.B: Aldolase B; fructose-1-phosphate accumulation causes hepatic and renal toxicity
options.C: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase; impaired gluconeogenesis causes lactic acidosis
options.D: Fructose-6-phosphate isomerase; excess fructose-6-phosphate inhibits glycolysis

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Hereditary Fructose Intolerance (HFI), caused by Aldolase B deficiency. When fructose is ingested, fructokinase converts fructose → fructose-1-phosphate (F1P). Normally, aldolase B cleaves F1P to DHAP and glyceraldehyde. Without aldolase B, F1P accumulates massively. F1P is toxic because: (1) It sequesters phosphate, depleting Pi and ATP (inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis → severe hypoglycemia). (2) It directly damages hepatocytes and proximal renal tubules (Fanconi syndrome). Treatment: eliminate fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol from diet. Option A: Fructokinase deficiency = essential fructosuria (benign condition) — fructose accumulates in blood/urine but is not toxic (no organ damage). Option C: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency presents with fasting lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia (impaired gluconeogenesis) — not triggered by fructose ingestion specifically. Option D: Fructose-6-phosphate isomerase deficiency is not a clinically significant IEM. Exam pearl: HFI vs. Essential fructosuria: HFI (aldolase B deficiency) is dangerous — fructose ingestion causes acute hypoglycemia and liver failure. Essential fructosuria (fructokinase deficiency) is benign — detected as reducing substance in urine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, muscle weakness, and sensorineural hearing loss. Muscle biopsy shows ragged red fibers on Gomori trichrome stain. Genetic analysis reveals a 4977 bp deletion in mitochondrial DNA. This condition demonstrates maternal inheritance. A 2-year-old sibling of the same mother is unaffected. Which phenomenon explains why siblings of the same affected mother can have different disease expression?

options.A: Mosaicism: the mitochondrial mutation is present in some nuclear chromosomes but not others
options.B: Heteroplasmy: each cell contains a mixture of mutant and wild-type mitochondrial DNA, and the proportion varies between tissues and individuals
options.C: Incomplete penetrance: the autosomal dominant mutation has variable expressivity in different family members
options.D: Genomic imprinting: the maternal allele is differentially methylated in the sibling

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Heteroplasmy. Mitochondrial genetics differs fundamentally from nuclear genetics: (1) Mitochondria have multiple copies of circular DNA (37 genes: 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs, 13 ETC/ATP synthase subunits). (2) When a cell divides, mitochondria are distributed randomly between daughter cells (mitotic segregation). (3) Heteroplasmy: a cell/individual carries a mixture of mutant and wild-type mtDNA. Disease manifests only when the proportion of mutant mtDNA exceeds a threshold (threshold effect), which varies by tissue (high-energy tissues — muscle, brain, heart — have lower thresholds). Since mitochondria are distributed randomly during oocyte development, each child of an affected mother may inherit a different ratio of mutant:wild-type mtDNA — explaining variable expression. Option A: Mosaicism refers to nuclear genetic heterogeneity in somatic cells, not mitochondrial genetics. Option C: Incomplete penetrance/variable expressivity applies to autosomal dominant disorders; this is mitochondrial. Option D: Genomic imprinting involves nuclear genes, not mtDNA. Exam pearl: Mitochondrial diseases — maternal inheritance (all children of affected mother are at risk; father never transmits). Classic diseases: MELAS (3243 A→G tRNA mutation), MERRF, LHON, Kearns-Sayre (large deletion like this case). Ragged red fibers = accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria beneath sarcolemma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman on long-term isoniazid therapy for latent tuberculosis develops peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, and seborrheic dermatitis around the eyes and mouth. Serum homocysteine is mildly elevated. Which vitamin deficiency is MOST likely, and what is the mechanism by which isoniazid causes it?

options.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency; isoniazid inhibits intrinsic factor secretion
options.B: Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency; isoniazid forms a hydrazone with pyridoxal, preventing its phosphorylation to the active PLP form
options.C: Folate deficiency; isoniazid inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
options.D: Niacin deficiency; isoniazid inhibits tryptophan conversion to niacin

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Isoniazid (INH) is a hydrazide that forms a covalent hydrazone complex with pyridoxal (vitamin B6 aldehyde form), trapping it and preventing its phosphorylation to pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP) — the active coenzyme form. PLP is required for: transaminase reactions, decarboxylation of amino acids, glycogen phosphorylase, delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (heme synthesis), cystathionine beta-synthase (hence elevated homocysteine). Clinical features of B6 deficiency: peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, seborrheic dermatitis, cheilosis, microcytic sideroblastic anemia, elevated homocysteine. Prophylaxis: pyridoxine 25–50 mg/day should be given with INH to all patients on long-term therapy, especially those at high risk (malnourished, elderly, diabetics, alcoholics). Option A: B12 deficiency is caused by pernicious anemia (IF deficiency) or diet; not the mechanism of INH. Option C: Methotrexate inhibits DHFR, not INH. Option D: While INH can minimally affect tryptophan-niacin conversion, the primary deficiency is B6. Exam pearl: Drugs causing B6 deficiency: INH, cycloserine, hydralazine, penicillamine. All bind PLP or pyridoxal.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
key_findings: Large macrophages (Gaucher cells) with crinkled tissue-paper or wrinkled silk cytoplasm
Eccentric nuclei displaced by storage material
No foamy appearance (distinguishes from Niemann-Pick cells)
Infiltration of bone marrow causing pancytopenia
Erlenmeyer flask deformity of distal femur on X-ray
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish woman presents with splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, bone pain, and easy bruising. Complete blood count shows pancytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy shows the cells seen in the image. Enzyme assay confirms glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase) deficiency. Which is the MOST effective disease-modifying treatment currently available for this condition?

options.A: Bone marrow transplantation as first-line therapy in all patients
options.B: Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with imiglucerase or velaglucerase alfa
options.C: High-dose corticosteroids to reduce macrophage activation
options.D: Substrate reduction therapy with miglustat as the sole first-line treatment

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — ERT with imiglucerase (modified recombinant glucocerebrosidase). Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disease. ERT delivers functional enzyme to macrophages via mannose receptors, clearing glucocerebroside accumulation. It effectively treats hematological (pancytopenia), hepatosplenic, and bone manifestations. It is the first-line treatment for moderate-to-severe Type I Gaucher disease. Option A: BMT is not first-line; it is considered only in refractory cases or Type III (neuronopathic) where ERT doesn't cross the blood-brain barrier. Option C: Corticosteroids have no role in treating Gaucher disease. Option D: Miglustat (substrate reduction therapy — inhibits glucosylceramide synthase) is used as an ALTERNATIVE when ERT is not feasible (oral route), not as sole first-line treatment. Eliglustat is a newer oral substrate reduction therapy approved as first-line for suitable patients. Exam pearl: Gaucher disease types: Type I (non-neuronopathic) most common — responds to ERT. Types II and III involve CNS — ERT does not help CNS. Gaucher cell appearance: wrinkled tissue paper/crinkled silk cytoplasm (vs. Niemann-Pick: foamy/sea-blue histiocytes). Gene: GBA (chromosome 1q21). Mutations: N370S (most common in Ashkenazi Jewish); L444P (neuronopathic forms).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, recurrent otitis media, and developmental regression. Urinary GAG excretion is elevated. Enzyme assay in fibroblasts shows absent alpha-L-iduronidase activity. The abnormal lysosomal enzymes in this disorder lack proper targeting signals. Which post-translational modification is defective in a related disorder (I-cell disease/Mucolipidosis II) that results in misrouting of lysosomal enzymes?

options.A: Defective sulfation of mannose residues on lysosomal enzymes
options.B: Defective addition of mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag due to absent GlcNAc-phosphotransferase
options.C: Defective signal peptide cleavage, preventing lysosomal enzyme entry into the ER
options.D: Defective O-glycosylation of serine residues on lysosomal hydrolases

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The question describes Hurler syndrome (MPS Type I, alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency). But the deeper question is about I-cell disease (Mucolipidosis II — GlcNAc-phosphotransferase deficiency). In normal lysosomal enzyme targeting: lysosomal enzymes are N-glycosylated in the ER, then in the cis-Golgi, GlcNAc-phosphotransferase adds GlcNAc-1-phosphate to mannose residues. Phosphodiesterase removes GlcNAc to expose mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag. M6P receptor on the trans-Golgi network recognizes M6P-tagged enzymes and routes them to lysosomes. In I-cell disease (GlcNAc-phosphotransferase deficiency): M6P tag cannot be added → lysosomal enzymes are secreted into blood (NOT delivered to lysosomes) → inclusions form in cells (I-cells). Option A: Mannose is phosphorylated (not sulfated) for lysosomal targeting. Option C: Signal peptide cleavage occurs cotranslationally for ALL secretory/membrane proteins — its defect would be non-specific. Option D: O-glycosylation is not the targeting signal for lysosomal enzymes. Exam pearl: M6P = the zip code for lysosomal targeting. I-cell disease = severe phenotype due to deficiency of ALL lysosomal enzymes. Serum lysosomal enzyme levels are very HIGH (enzymes secreted into blood). Hurler vs. Scheie: both α-L-iduronidase deficiency but different mutation severity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old woman with colon cancer is treated with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). The drug is converted intracellularly to FdUMP. FdUMP covalently binds thymidylate synthase in the presence of N5,N10-methyleneTHF, inhibiting the enzyme. Which DIRECT consequence of this inhibition results in cancer cell death?

options.A: Decreased dATP production, impairing DNA replication at the polymerase level
options.B: Decreased dTMP (deoxythymidylate) synthesis, causing thymineless death by impairing DNA replication
options.C: Increased dUMP accumulation which directly inhibits DNA polymerase delta
options.D: Depletion of N5,N10-methylene-THF, impairing both purine and pyrimidine synthesis simultaneously

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Thymidylate synthase catalyzes: dUMP + N5,N10-methylene-THF → dTMP + DHF. dTMP is phosphorylated to dTTP, which is incorporated into DNA. 5-FU → FdUMP: forms a covalent ternary complex with thymidylate synthase + N5,N10-methylene-THF → enzyme is irreversibly inhibited. Without dTMP: dTTP is depleted → DNA synthesis/repair is impaired → uracil is misincorporated into DNA → strand breaks and cell death ('thymineless death'). This preferentially kills rapidly dividing cancer cells. Option A: dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate) synthesis is a purine pathway; thymidylate synthase affects only dTMP (pyrimidine). Option C: dUMP does accumulate, but direct DNA polymerase delta inhibition is NOT the mechanism — it is the downstream shortage of dTTP and uracil misincorporation. Option D: THF is trapped as DHF; N5,N10-methylene-THF is depleted at the thymidylate synthase step, but 5-FU's primary effect is on pyrimidine synthesis; purine synthesis is not the primary target. Exam pearl: 5-FU is used in colorectal, breast, gastric cancers. Leucovorin (folinic acid) POTENTIATES 5-FU by increasing the cellular pool of N5,N10-methylene-THF, stabilizing the ternary complex. Side effects: myelosuppression, mucositis, hand-foot syndrome. Bioactivation requires uridine phosphorylase and thymidine kinase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A researcher studies the effect of a new compound that irreversibly activates adenylyl cyclase in beta cells of the pancreas. This activation is analogous to the mechanism of Gs protein activation by cholera toxin. What is the DIRECT downstream effect on insulin secretion and the biochemical basis?

options.A: Decreased insulin secretion because cAMP inhibits protein kinase A in beta cells
options.B: Increased insulin secretion because elevated cAMP activates PKA → phosphorylates voltage-gated Ca2+ channels → increased Ca2+ influx → exocytosis of insulin granules
options.C: No change in insulin secretion because insulin secretion is glucose-dependent only
options.D: Decreased insulin secretion because cAMP activates phosphodiesterase to degrade itself rapidly

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The cAMP-PKA pathway in pancreatic beta cells potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS). Adenylyl cyclase activation (analogous to GLP-1 receptor activation or cholera toxin on Gs) → ↑ cAMP → ↑ PKA activity → PKA phosphorylates multiple targets including voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and the exocytic machinery → ↑ Ca2+ influx → insulin granule exocytosis. This is the mechanism exploited by GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) and DPP-4 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes treatment. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα, locking it in active state → constitutive adenylyl cyclase activation → massive cAMP elevation. In enterocytes this causes Cl- secretion and diarrhea; the same mechanism in beta cells would stimulate insulin release. Option A: cAMP ACTIVATES PKA; PKA does not inhibit insulin secretion. Option C: cAMP significantly potentiates insulin secretion; glucose is necessary but not the only signal. Option D: Phosphodiesterase degrades cAMP (it's a regulatory check), but this is not the direct downstream effect of adenylyl cyclase activation. Exam pearl: GLP-1 receptor agonists work via this pathway. Cholera toxin vs. Pertussis toxin: Cholera → ADP-ribosylates Gsα (activates) → ↑ cAMP. Pertussis → ADP-ribosylates Giα (prevents inhibition) → ↑ cAMP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man on long-term methotrexate therapy for rheumatoid arthritis develops megaloblastic anemia, elevated homocysteine, and mouth ulcers. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Which metabolite most directly explains the megaloblastic anemia in this patient?

options.A: Accumulated dihydrofolate (DHF) directly damages RBC precursors
options.B: Depletion of tetrahydrofolate (THF) → insufficient N5,N10-methylene-THF for dTMP synthesis → impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells
options.C: Depletion of THF → reduced remethylation of homocysteine to methionine → reduced SAM → impaired methylation reactions
options.D: Accumulated methotrexate-polyglutamate directly inhibits hemoglobin synthesis

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Methotrexate inhibits DHFR → DHF cannot be reduced to THF → cellular folate pool is trapped as DHF. Without THF, N5,N10-methylene-THF (required for thymidylate synthase to make dTMP) is depleted → dTMP → dTTP deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis → megaloblastic changes in rapidly proliferating cells (RBC precursors, GI epithelium). This is 'thymineless death' in erythroid precursors → megaloblastic anemia. The megaloblastic anemia is primarily due to impaired DNA synthesis (dTTP deficiency), not impaired methylation. Option A: Accumulated DHF is not directly cytotoxic to RBC precursors. Option C: Reduced remethylation (leading to hyperhomocysteinemia) does occur with methotrexate, but the megaloblastic anemia is primarily a DNA synthesis issue, not an SAM deficiency issue. Option D: Methotrexate-polyglutamates are the active retained form intracellularly, but they don't directly impair hemoglobin synthesis. Exam pearl: Treatment of methotrexate toxicity: Leucovorin (folinic acid, 5-formyl-THF) — bypasses DHFR block by providing pre-formed THF. For high-dose methotrexate: 'leucovorin rescue' protocol. Methotrexate also inhibits thymidylate synthase and ATIC (purine synthesis) via its polyglutamate forms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man is found to have a monoclonal immunoglobulin spike on serum protein electrophoresis (M-spike in gamma region). Bone marrow biopsy shows 60% plasma cells. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation confirm IgG kappa monoclonal protein. Urine shows Bence Jones proteins. Which type of protein do Bence Jones proteins represent?

options.A: Intact monoclonal IgG immunoglobulins filtered by the kidney
options.B: Free monoclonal light chains (kappa or lambda) produced in excess and filtered by glomeruli
options.C: Heavy chain fragments from IgG degradation
options.D: Beta-2-microglobulin shed from plasma cell membranes

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. In multiple myeloma, malignant plasma cells produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin. In many cases, excess free light chains (either kappa or lambda, not both) are produced and secreted. These free light chains (molecular weight ~22 kDa) are small enough to be filtered by glomeruli and appear in urine as Bence Jones proteins. Bence Jones proteins have a characteristic thermosolvability property — they precipitate at 45–60°C and redissolve at 100°C. Free light chains can cause tubular damage (light chain cast nephropathy — myeloma kidney), AL amyloidosis, and light chain deposition disease. Option A: Intact IgG (~150 kDa) is too large to be filtered by normal glomeruli. Option C: Heavy chain fragments appear in heavy chain diseases (Franklin disease, etc.) — different condition. Option D: Beta-2-microglobulin is a prognostic marker in myeloma but is not Bence Jones protein. Exam pearl: Bence Jones proteins: free monoclonal light chains in urine. Urine dipstick may be NEGATIVE (detects albumin, not free light chains) — need SSA test or urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation. Serum free light chain (FLC) assay is more sensitive. Kappa:lambda ratio >26 or <0.01 suggests malignancy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with painful peripheral neuropathy, retinopathy, and cataracts despite being on adequate insulin therapy. His HbA1c is 9.2%. The pathophysiology of these complications involves the polyol pathway. Which statement BEST explains why sorbitol accumulates in these tissues and causes damage?

options.A: Aldose reductase has a high Km for glucose and only becomes active when glucose is extremely high; sorbitol exits cells freely
options.B: Aldose reductase has a low Km and high affinity for glucose; sorbitol cannot exit cells efficiently, causing osmotic damage and NADPH depletion
options.C: Sorbitol dehydrogenase is overactive in diabetic tissues, converting sorbitol to fructose faster than it can be cleared
options.D: The polyol pathway is the primary source of cellular energy in nervous tissue during hyperglycemia

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The polyol (sorbitol) pathway: Glucose → Sorbitol (aldose reductase, using NADPH) → Fructose (sorbitol dehydrogenase, producing NADH). In hyperglycemia, excess glucose enters the polyol pathway (insulin-independent tissues: retina, lens, kidney, Schwann cells, endothelium). Aldose reductase has a high affinity (low Km) for glucose — it is active even at normal glucose concentrations in these tissues. Sorbitol is a polar molecule that cannot cross cell membranes easily → accumulates → osmotic damage. Additionally: NADPH is consumed → reduced regeneration of GSH → oxidative stress. Option A: Aldose reductase actually has LOW Km (high affinity) — the opposite of this option. Option C: Sorbitol dehydrogenase is not overactive; sorbitol accumulates precisely because this conversion is limited or overwhelmed. Option D: The polyol pathway is not a primary energy source; glycolysis is. Exam pearl: Tissues susceptible to diabetic complications are insulin-independent for glucose uptake (don't need GLUT4): retina (GLUT1), lens (diffusion), kidney, peripheral nerves (Schwann cells). Aldose reductase inhibitors (e.g., epalrestat) are used clinically to reduce sorbitol accumulation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A forensic scientist uses a technique to identify a murder suspect from a blood stain. She amplifies specific STR (short tandem repeat) loci from minute quantities of DNA and generates a unique DNA fingerprint. After PCR amplification, she uses gel electrophoresis to separate bands. The suspect's profile matches the evidence DNA at all 15 loci tested. Which feature of PCR makes it suitable for this application?

options.A: PCR can only amplify RNA templates, making it ideal for forensic applications
options.B: PCR exponentially amplifies specific DNA sequences from minute template amounts, enabling analysis of nanogram quantities of degraded forensic DNA
options.C: PCR requires fresh, undegraded DNA and cannot work from aged specimens
options.D: PCR amplification produces blunt-ended, ligase-ready fragments suitable for immediate cloning

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies DNA exponentially (2^n copies after n cycles) from minute starting templates. Forensic applications succeed because: (1) Only nanogram or even picogram amounts of DNA are needed. (2) Short STR sequences (100–400 bp) can be amplified even from partially degraded DNA. (3) High specificity — primers hybridize only to target sequences. Temperature cycling: Denaturation (94–96°C) → Annealing (50–65°C, primer binding) → Extension (72°C, Taq polymerase synthesis). Taq polymerase (thermostable, from Thermus aquaticus) withstands repeated denaturation cycles. Option A: Standard PCR amplifies DNA templates. RT-PCR (reverse transcriptase PCR) amplifies RNA by first making cDNA; this is not standard forensic PCR. Option C: PCR can work with aged or degraded DNA, especially with short-fragment amplification strategies — this is a STRENGTH, not a limitation. Option D: Taq polymerase adds a 3' adenine overhang (not blunt ends), which is exploited in TA cloning; this is not the primary forensic advantage. Exam pearl: PCR inventor: Kary Mullis (Nobel Prize 1993). Applications: forensics, prenatal diagnosis, pathogen detection, oncology (EGFR mutation testing), quantitative PCR (qPCR) for viral load measurement.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman with osteoarthritis and a history of peptic ulcer disease needs an NSAID. Her physician prescribes celecoxib instead of ibuprofen. Both drugs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, but celecoxib has a lower risk of GI ulceration. Which biochemical distinction between COX isoforms explains this differential effect?

options.A: COX-1 is inducible and produces prostaglandins that damage the gastric mucosa
options.B: COX-2 is constitutive in the stomach and its inhibition causes ulcers; COX-1 is inducible at sites of inflammation
options.C: COX-1 is constitutive in gastric mucosa (producing cytoprotective prostaglandins) and platelets; COX-2 is inducible at inflammatory sites — selective COX-2 inhibition spares gastric protection
options.D: Celecoxib directly blocks leukotriene synthesis, providing GI mucosal protection

questions.explanation: Correct answer: C. Cyclooxygenase (COX) has two main isoforms: COX-1 (constitutive): present in most tissues including gastric mucosa (produces PGE2 and PGI2 — protective prostaglandins that stimulate mucus/bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow) and platelets (TXA2 synthesis). COX-2 (inducible): induced by inflammatory stimuli (cytokines, growth factors); produces prostaglandins at sites of inflammation and pain. Non-selective NSAIDs (ibuprofen, aspirin, naproxen) inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2 → GI mucosal damage (loss of COX-1-mediated protection) + anti-inflammatory effect. Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) inhibit only COX-2 → anti-inflammatory + analgesic effect WITHOUT GI mucosal protection being lost. However: selective COX-2 inhibitors carry increased cardiovascular risk (because prostacyclin PGI2 production from COX-2 in endothelium is reduced, while platelet TXA2 from COX-1 is unaffected → prothrombotic imbalance). Options A, B, D are incorrect based on the above. Exam pearl: Aspirin uniquely IRREVERSIBLY inhibits COX (acetylation) — important in cardiovascular prophylaxis. All other NSAIDs are reversible competitive inhibitors. Low-dose aspirin inhibits platelet TXA2 (platelets can't synthesize new COX). COX-2 also has constitutive expression in kidney, brain, and endothelium.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A patient with Parkinson's disease is started on levodopa (L-DOPA) combined with carbidopa. Carbidopa is added to the regimen to enhance the therapeutic effect. Which enzyme does carbidopa inhibit, and why does this combination increase brain dopamine levels?

options.A: DOPA decarboxylase peripherally; preventing peripheral conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine, allowing more L-DOPA to cross the blood-brain barrier
options.B: Monoamine oxidase (MAO) centrally; preventing dopamine degradation in the brain
options.C: Tyrosine hydroxylase peripherally; reducing peripheral dopamine synthesis to redirect substrate centrally
options.D: Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) peripherally; preventing dopamine methylation

questions.explanation: Correct answer: A. Carbidopa is a peripheral DOPA decarboxylase (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase) inhibitor that does NOT cross the blood-brain barrier. Without carbidopa: L-DOPA is largely converted to dopamine in peripheral tissues before reaching the brain → peripheral side effects (nausea, vomiting, cardiac arrhythmias) + reduced CNS dopamine. With carbidopa: peripheral conversion is inhibited → more L-DOPA reaches the brain → central DOPA decarboxylase converts it to dopamine in the striatum → improved Parkinson's symptoms. The dose of L-DOPA can be reduced by 75% when carbidopa is added. Option B: MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline) are used adjunctively but are not carbidopa. Option C: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis (tyrosine → DOPA). Carbidopa doesn't inhibit this. Option D: COMT inhibitors (entacapone, tolcapone) are another drug class used in Parkinson's — also reduce peripheral L-DOPA degradation but by a different mechanism. Exam pearl: Catecholamine synthesis pathway: Tyrosine → DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting) → Dopamine (DOPA decarboxylase) → Norepinephrine (dopamine beta-hydroxylase) → Epinephrine (PNMT). Cofactors: tyrosine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4); DOPA decarboxylase requires PLP (B6).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old medical student fasts for 72 hours as an experiment. Serial blood glucose measurements show glucose stabilizing at 60–70 mg/dL after 48 hours. At this point, which COMBINATION of metabolic adaptations is maintaining euglycemia?

options.A: High glycogen stores in liver and muscle providing sustained glucose release
options.B: Active gluconeogenesis from amino acids (mainly alanine and glutamine from muscle proteolysis) and glycerol (from lipolysis), combined with reduced glucose utilization by the brain shifting to ketone bodies
options.C: Activation of the Cori cycle where lactate from all tissues is converted to glucose by the kidneys exclusively
options.D: Ketone bodies are directly converted to glucose by the liver, maintaining blood glucose

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. In prolonged fasting (>24 hours), liver glycogen is depleted within 12–24 hours. After this: (1) Gluconeogenesis becomes primary: substrates = alanine and glutamine (from muscle proteolysis via the glucose-alanine cycle), glycerol (from adipose tissue lipolysis). (2) The liver produces ketone bodies from fatty acids → the brain progressively shifts to ketone body utilization (reduces glucose demand from ~120 g/day to ~40 g/day after adaptation). (3) Lipolysis provides fatty acids → fuel for muscle and liver. This combination maintains blood glucose in the 60–70 mg/dL range. Option A: Liver glycogen is depleted by 24–36 hours; muscle glycogen does not contribute to blood glucose (no glucose-6-phosphatase in muscle). Option C: The Cori cycle operates between muscle and liver; the kidneys contribute to gluconeogenesis but are not the exclusive organ; 'exclusively' makes this wrong. Option D: Ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) CANNOT be converted to glucose — they are derived from acetyl-CoA, which cannot enter gluconeogenesis (acetyl-CoA carboxylase and loss of carbon as CO2 in the TCA cycle). Exam pearl: Gluconeogenic precursors: Alanine (from muscle), Glutamine (from muscle → kidney GNG in prolonged fasting), Glycerol (from triglycerides), Lactate (from RBCs and exercising muscle — Cori cycle). Odd-chain fatty acids → propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → gluconeogenesis (minor).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A biochemist adds 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) to isolated mitochondria that are actively oxidizing NADH. She observes that oxygen consumption INCREASES while ATP synthesis FALLS to near zero. Membrane potential (ΔΨm) across the inner mitochondrial membrane collapses. Which term BEST describes DNP's mechanism?

options.A: Competitive inhibitor of Complex I, blocking NADH oxidation
options.B: Proton ionophore/uncoupler that dissipates the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, uncoupling electron transport from ATP synthesis
options.C: Inhibitor of ATP synthase (Complex V) that prevents proton re-entry into the matrix
options.D: Inhibitor of the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT), preventing ADP/ATP exchange

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) is a lipid-soluble weak acid. It can accept protons on the cytoplasmic face of the inner mitochondrial membrane (becomes neutral, lipid-soluble), diffuse through the lipid bilayer, and release protons on the matrix side (becomes charged again). This bypasses ATP synthase, dissipating the proton gradient (proton motive force) as heat. Consequences: ETC continues running (O2 consumption increases) to try to restore the gradient, but since protons bypass ATP synthase, ATP synthesis falls. Energy is released as heat. DNP was historically used as a weight-loss drug in the 1930s — caused hyperthermia and deaths. Option A: Complex I inhibitors (rotenone) would block NADH oxidation and DECREASE O2 consumption. Option C: ATP synthase inhibitors (oligomycin) would decrease O2 consumption (state 3→4 respiration) and block ATP synthesis — O2 consumption does NOT increase. Option D: ANT inhibitors (atractyloside, bongkrekic acid) block ADP-ATP exchange — O2 consumption decreases. Exam pearl: Uncouplers increase O2 consumption + decrease ATP + increase heat production. Physiological uncoupler: UCP-1 (thermogenin) in brown adipose tissue — generates heat for thermogenesis (non-shivering thermogenesis in neonates and cold-adapted organisms).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old strict vegetarian woman presents with megaloblastic anemia. MCV is 118 fL. She has subacute combined degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord — posterior and lateral column involvement. Serum B12 is very low; serum folate is normal. Schilling test is abnormal in both phases (with and without intrinsic factor). Which ADDITIONAL biochemical finding is MOST specific for B12 deficiency (differentiating it from folate deficiency)?

options.A: Elevated serum homocysteine
options.B: Elevated urine and serum methylmalonic acid (MMA)
options.C: Hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear
options.D: Low serum iron and ferritin

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Elevated methylmalonic acid (MMA). B12 is required as a cofactor for TWO enzymes: (1) Methionine synthase: homocysteine + methyl-THF → methionine (requires methylcobalamin) → elevated homocysteine in B12 deficiency. (2) Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase: methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (requires adenosylcobalamin) → elevated MMA in B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency also elevates homocysteine (methionine synthase requires both B12 and MTHF), but does NOT elevate MMA (folate is not involved in the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction). Therefore, elevated MMA is SPECIFIC for B12 deficiency. Option A: Homocysteine is elevated in both B12 AND folate deficiency — not specific. Option C: Hypersegmented neutrophils occur in megaloblastic anemia from either B12 or folate deficiency. Option D: Iron deficiency is a separate cause of anemia (microcytic); unrelated here. Exam pearl: B12 deficiency specific markers: elevated MMA + elevated homocysteine + low serum B12. Folate deficiency: elevated homocysteine ONLY (MMA normal). Neurological manifestations (SACD) occur ONLY with B12 deficiency (not folate). SACD is due to impaired myelin synthesis (requires SAM from methionine cycle). Treating B12 deficiency with folate alone can CORRECT anemia but WORSEN SACD — dangerous trap.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 7-day-old neonate presents with poor feeding, alternating hypotonia and hypertonia, seizures, and a distinctive sweet maple-syrup odor of the urine. Plasma amino acid analysis shows markedly elevated leucine, isoleucine, and valine. The urine DNPH test is positive. Which enzyme is deficient and which cofactor does it require?

options.A: Phenylalanine hydroxylase; tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
options.B: Branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex (BCKDH); thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), lipoic acid, FAD, NAD+, CoA
options.C: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase; biotin
options.D: Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase; FAD

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — BCKDH complex deficiency = Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD). Branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) are first transaminated to their corresponding alpha-keto acids, which are then decarboxylated by the BCKDH complex (analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase complex). BCKDH requires five cofactors: TPP (E1 component), lipoic acid (E2), FAD (E3), NAD+ (E3), and CoA (E2). Without BCKDH, alpha-keto acids accumulate → maple syrup odor (from sotolone, derived from alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate from isoleucine). Leucine is most neurotoxic (competitive inhibitor of brain large neutral amino acid transport). DNPH (dinitrophenylhydrazine) test detects keto acids in urine. Option A: PKU — phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Option C: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase — deficiency causes propionic acidemia (elevated propionate, not BCAA). Option D: Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency causes isovaleric acidemia — sweaty feet odor, not maple syrup. Exam pearl: MSUD treatment: Dietary restriction of BCAA (special formula). Thiamine-responsive MSUD exists (high-dose B1 helps in some mutations). Emergency treatment of acute crisis: dialysis to rapidly remove BCAA. Leucine is the most toxic amino acid — causes cerebral edema and brain damage.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A virology laboratory confirms HIV infection in a patient using a Western blot test after an initial positive ELISA. The Western blot shows bands at p24, gp41, and gp120. Which statement BEST describes what a Western blot detects and why it is used as a confirmatory test?

options.A: Western blot detects viral RNA in patient blood using complementary DNA probes
options.B: Western blot detects patient antibodies against specific viral proteins by separating viral proteins by molecular weight, transferring to membrane, and probing with patient serum — high specificity due to antigen-specific detection
options.C: Western blot detects viral proteins using monoclonal antibodies against conserved HIV epitopes
options.D: Western blot amplifies viral DNA sequences to confirm proviral integration in T lymphocytes
