questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Western blot (immunoblot) procedure: (1) Viral antigens (HIV proteins) are separated by SDS-PAGE according to molecular weight. (2) Proteins are electrotransferred to a nitrocellulose or PVDF membrane. (3) Patient's serum is added — if the patient has anti-HIV antibodies, they bind to specific HIV proteins. (4) Secondary antibody (enzyme-conjugated anti-human IgG) produces visible bands. Positive result requires bands at: p24 (capsid) AND gp41 or gp120/gp160 (envelope). High specificity because individual protein bands are identified — much more specific than ELISA (which detects total anti-HIV antibodies and has more cross-reactivity). Option A: Detecting viral RNA uses RT-PCR or Northern blot. Option C: This describes an ELISA or immunohistochemistry for viral antigens, not patient antibodies. Option D: Detecting proviral DNA uses PCR. Exam pearl: Molecular biology blots mnemonic — SNoW DRoP: Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = Protein. HIV diagnosis algorithm: ELISA (sensitive screening) → if positive → Western blot confirmation (specific) → if indeterminate → NAT (nucleic acid test/viral RNA load).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old obese woman undergoes ileal resection for Crohn's disease. Six months later, she develops steatorrhea, deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and hyperoxaluria. Which mechanism explains the hyperoxaluria in this patient?

options.A: Increased hepatic oxalate synthesis due to cholesterol accumulation after bile acid loss
options.B: Colonic absorption of unbound (free) oxalate — normally bound to calcium in the gut, but excess fatty acids in the colon bind calcium preferentially, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed
options.C: Reduced renal oxalate excretion due to vitamin D deficiency-induced hypocalciuria
options.D: Increased dietary oxalate intake due to compensatory diet changes after surgery

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Enteric hyperoxaluria (secondary hyperoxaluria). In normal physiology, dietary oxalate binds calcium in the intestine to form insoluble calcium oxalate → excreted in feces. After ileal resection: (1) Bile acids cannot be reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation interrupted) → excess bile acids and fatty acids reach the colon. (2) Fatty acids in the colon bind calcium (saponification) preferentially → free oxalate is NOT bound to calcium → increased free oxalate is absorbed by colonocytes → hyperoxaluria → calcium oxalate kidney stones. This is called enteric/secondary hyperoxaluria. Additionally: fat malabsorption → steatorrhea; fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Option A: Cholesterol accumulation and oxalate synthesis link does not exist as described. Option C: Vitamin D deficiency affects calcium metabolism but hypocalciuria would actually reduce calcium oxalate stone risk. Option D: While diet can affect oxalate intake, the primary mechanism here is the saponification of calcium by excess fat. Exam pearl: Enteric hyperoxaluria after ileal resection or bariatric surgery. Calcium oxalate stones most common in primary hyperoxaluria (autosomal recessive, glyoxalate metabolism enzyme deficiency) — don't confuse with secondary/enteric hyperoxaluria. Management: low-fat diet, calcium supplementation with meals (to bind oxalate in gut), low-oxalate diet, hydration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis. It is allosterically activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP) and inhibited by ATP and citrate. In a hepatocyte during fasting: glucagon is elevated, insulin is low. Glucagon activates adenylyl cyclase → PKA. PKA phosphorylates phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (PFK-2/FBPase-2) bifunctional enzyme. What is the NET effect on glycolysis in this fasted hepatocyte?

options.A: Increased glycolysis because phosphorylation activates PFK-2, increasing F-2,6-BP, which activates PFK-1
options.B: Decreased glycolysis because phosphorylation activates FBPase-2 activity (and inactivates PFK-2 activity), decreasing F-2,6-BP levels, thereby removing allosteric activation of PFK-1
options.C: No change in glycolysis because F-2,6-BP is only relevant in muscle, not liver
options.D: Increased gluconeogenesis due to PKA phosphorylating PFK-1 directly, converting it to an inactive form

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2 has two activities that are reciprocally regulated by phosphorylation: In FED state (high insulin): PFK-2 activity is active (dephosphorylated form) → makes F-2,6-BP → F-2,6-BP allosterically activates PFK-1 → glycolysis ON. In FASTED state (glucagon → PKA → phosphorylation of bifunctional enzyme): FBPase-2 activity is activated; PFK-2 activity is INACTIVATED → F-2,6-BP is degraded → PFK-1 loses its most potent allosteric activator → glycolysis is reduced → gluconeogenesis is favored (F-2,6-BP also inhibits FBPase-1, so its reduction also disinhibits FBPase-1 → promotes gluconeogenesis). Option A: Phosphorylation INACTIVATES PFK-2 (in liver) — the opposite. Option C: F-2,6-BP is actually most important in liver (hormonal regulation); in muscle, AMP is the primary regulator. Option D: PKA does not directly phosphorylate PFK-1; it acts through the bifunctional enzyme. Exam pearl: This is the MASTER SWITCH of glucose metabolism in the liver. F-2,6-BP: highest levels after feeding (promotes glycolysis, inhibits gluconeogenesis). Lowest levels during fasting (promotes gluconeogenesis). CRITICAL exam concept.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 3-day-old neonate born to a mother with no prenatal care presents with jaundice, poor feeding, and E. coli sepsis. Blood glucose is low. Urine reducing substance is positive but glucose oxidase is negative. Newborn metabolic screening is pending. Which immediate management step is MOST critical for this neonate?

options.A: Administer IV galactose infusion to restore energy
options.B: Immediately discontinue all lactose/galactose-containing feeds and switch to a galactose-free formula
options.C: Start empiric antibiotic therapy only and await metabolic screening results
options.D: Perform exchange transfusion to remove accumulated galactose

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. The presentation strongly suggests Galactosemia (likely GALT deficiency/Type I). The clinical triad: jaundice + hypoglycemia + E. coli neonatal sepsis (galactose accumulation impairs neutrophil killing of E. coli). Urine reducing substance positive but glucose oxidase negative confirms a non-glucose reducing sugar (galactose). Immediate management: STOP galactose/lactose-containing feeds (standard infant formula and breast milk contain lactose = glucose + galactose). Switch to a galactose-free formula (soy-based in infancy, though soy also contains some galactose precursors — casein hydrolysate formula is best). Also start antibiotics for E. coli sepsis. Option A: IV galactose would worsen toxicity — the patient cannot metabolize it. Option C: Waiting for screening results while continuing galactose feeds would cause progressive organ damage. Screening results can take days. Option D: Exchange transfusion is not standard initial management; dietary elimination is the key. Exam pearl: E. coli sepsis in a jaundiced neonate = think galactosemia. Galactose-1-phosphate accumulation impairs leukocyte bactericidal activity, predisposing to gram-negative sepsis. Long-term complications despite treatment: intellectual disability, premature ovarian failure (in girls), speech problems — galactose-1-phosphate accumulation in utero (from maternal galactose) causes prenatal injury even with postnatal dietary management.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: An investigator studies de novo fatty acid synthesis in rat liver hepatocytes after a high-carbohydrate meal. She labels acetate (as acetyl-CoA) with 14C and tracks its incorporation into palmitate. The rate-limiting enzyme is acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC). Which allosteric regulator ACTIVATES ACC, and which covalent modification INACTIVATES it?

options.A: Activated by palmitoyl-CoA (product inhibition); inactivated by AMP-kinase-mediated dephosphorylation
options.B: Activated by citrate (allosteric activator); inactivated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-mediated phosphorylation
options.C: Activated by malonyl-CoA; inactivated by insulin-stimulated phosphorylation
options.D: Activated by glucagon via cAMP; inactivated by palmitoyl-CoA binding

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) catalyzes: Acetyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP → Malonyl-CoA (committed step, rate-limiting in fatty acid synthesis). Regulation: Allosteric ACTIVATION: Citrate (from TCA cycle — signals excess acetyl-CoA and energy sufficiency — citrate is the cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA donor for FA synthesis, transported as citrate from mitochondria). Citrate promotes polymerization of ACC from inactive dimers to active filamentous form. Allosteric INHIBITION: Palmitoyl-CoA (end product inhibition — when FA synthesis is complete). Covalent INACTIVATION: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) phosphorylates ACC → inactive (AMPK is activated when AMP is high — i.e., energy depletion; statin side effects on muscle activate AMPK). Also PKA (glucagon signaling) phosphorylates ACC → inactive. Covalent ACTIVATION: Insulin activates phosphatase → dephosphorylates ACC → active. Option A: Palmitoyl-CoA inhibits (doesn't activate); AMPK phosphorylation inactivates (not dephosphorylation). Option C: Malonyl-CoA is the product, not an activator. Option D: Glucagon INHIBITS (not activates) fatty acid synthesis. Exam pearl: Malonyl-CoA (product of ACC) also inhibits CPT-I (carnitine palmitoyltransferase I) — preventing fatty acid transport into mitochondria for oxidation. This ensures that FA synthesis and FA oxidation don't occur simultaneously (reciprocal regulation).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms (confusion, psychosis), and dark urine after alcohol consumption and starting oral contraceptives. Urinary ALA and PBG are markedly elevated during attacks. Between attacks she is normal. Skin photosensitivity is absent. Which porphyria does this BEST represent, and which enzyme is deficient?

options.A: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT); uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
options.B: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP); hydroxymethylbilane synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase)
options.C: Erythropoietic Protoporphyria; ferrochelatase
options.D: Variegate Porphyria; protoporphyrinogen oxidase

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP), deficiency of HMBS (hydroxymethylbilane synthase = porphobilinogen deaminase). AIP features: Episodic attacks (triggered by drugs — barbiturates, OCP, alcohol, fasting, infection). NO skin photosensitivity (no porphyrin accumulation in skin — intermediate porphyrins don't accumulate beyond PBG). Triad: Abdominal pain (colicky) + Neuropsychiatric symptoms + Dark/port-wine urine (PBG polymerizes spontaneously to dark pigments). Elevated urinary ALA and PBG during attacks. Option A: PCT — presents with skin blistering and fragility on sun-exposed areas; uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase; NO acute attacks. Option C: Erythropoietic protoporphyria — severe photosensitivity in childhood; ferrochelatase deficiency; NO acute attacks. Option D: Variegate porphyria — BOTH acute attacks AND skin photosensitivity (protoporphyrinogen oxidase). Exam pearl: Mnemonic for porphyria drugs to AVOID in AIP: 'Four Bs' — Barbiturates, Booze (alcohol), Bactrim (sulfonamides), Birth control pills. Also rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine. SAFE drugs: Morphine, beta-blockers, aspirin, penicillin. Acute attacks treated with: IV heme (hematin/heme arginate) — suppresses ALA synthase-1; IV dextrose; pain management.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A molecular biologist uses EcoRI to digest both a plasmid and a gene of interest. EcoRI cuts the sequence G↓AATTC, producing overhanging single-stranded ends (5'-AATT-3' overhangs). She ligates the gene into the plasmid with DNA ligase. When both the plasmid and insert are cut with the same enzyme, what type of ends are generated, and why does this facilitate efficient ligation?

options.A: Blunt ends; they allow any two DNA fragments to ligate regardless of sequence
options.B: Sticky ends (cohesive ends); the complementary single-stranded overhangs from the same restriction enzyme base-pair with each other, increasing ligation efficiency and directionality
options.C: 3' recessed ends; they require T4 polynucleotide kinase before ligation
options.D: Phosphorothioate ends; resistant to exonuclease digestion

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Restriction endonucleases like EcoRI cut DNA asymmetrically within palindromic sequences, generating 5' overhangs (sticky/cohesive ends). EcoRI creates: 5'-G + AATTC-3' / 3'-CTTAA + G-5' → 5' AATT overhangs. When both insert and vector are cut with EcoRI, identical 5'-AATT overhangs are generated. These complementary overhangs base-pair with each other (AATT pairs with TTAA complement), bringing ends into close proximity → DNA ligase seals the nick. This is more efficient than blunt-end ligation because: (1) Complementary overhangs have a higher local effective concentration for annealing. (2) The enzyme provides directionality when two DIFFERENT restriction enzymes are used (directional cloning). Option A: Blunt ends (produced by enzymes like EcoRV, SmaI) can ligate but are much less efficient. Option C: 5' overhangs have 5' phosphates already; T4 PNK is needed to add 5' phosphates to blunt ends or 3'-recessed ends lacking them. Option D: Phosphorothioate modifications are used for antisense oligonucleotides, not standard restriction cloning. Exam pearl: Restriction enzymes recognize palindromic sequences (read same 5'→3' on both strands). Type II restriction enzymes are used in molecular cloning. Southern blot uses restriction enzyme digestion + gel electrophoresis + hybridization with labeled probe.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: An 18-month-old child presents with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, joint stiffness, and developmental delay. Urine shows elevated dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. Enzyme assay confirms alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency. Compared to Hurler syndrome (MPS I-H), Scheie syndrome (MPS I-S) has the same enzyme deficiency but a much milder phenotype with primarily joint and corneal involvement and normal intelligence. What BEST explains this phenotypic difference between allelic disorders?

options.A: Scheie is caused by deficiency of a different enzyme (iduronate-2-sulfatase)
options.B: Different mutations in the same IDUA gene result in different residual enzyme activity, with milder mutations in Scheie causing higher residual enzyme activity and milder GAG accumulation
options.C: Scheie syndrome has X-linked inheritance, protecting females from severe disease
options.D: In Scheie syndrome, dermatan sulfate (not heparan sulfate) accumulates preferentially, avoiding brain toxicity

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Both Hurler (MPS I-H) and Scheie (MPS I-S) syndromes are caused by mutations in the IDUA gene encoding alpha-L-iduronidase. They are allelic disorders — same gene, different mutations. In Hurler syndrome: severe loss-of-function mutations → near-zero enzyme activity → severe multi-system disease with intellectual disability, corneal clouding, dysostosis multiplex, death in 1st decade. In Scheie syndrome: milder mutations → some residual enzyme activity → slower GAG accumulation → milder phenotype with normal intelligence, primarily joint stiffness and corneal clouding. Hurler-Scheie compound heterozygotes have intermediate severity. Option A: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency = Hunter syndrome (MPS II, X-linked) — completely different enzyme. Option C: Both Hurler and Scheie are autosomal recessive — neither is X-linked. Option D: Both accumulate heparan sulfate AND dermatan sulfate; heparan sulfate is the primary neurotoxic species. Exam pearl: Hunter syndrome (MPS II) = X-linked, iduronate-2-sulfatase, NO corneal clouding (vs. Hurler which has corneal clouding). Mnemonic: Hunter has no Hurler in his eyes (no corneal clouding). Both accumulate heparan sulfate + dermatan sulfate. ERT available for Hurler (laronidase) and Hunter (idursulfase).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A researcher studying oxidative stress finds that superoxide (O2•−) generated by Complex I leak is rapidly converted to H2O2 by superoxide dismutase (SOD). H2O2 is then detoxified. In the presence of Fe2+ ions, H2O2 produces a highly reactive species via the Fenton reaction. A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis has excess free iron. Which reactive oxygen species is MOST directly generated by the Fenton reaction, and what cellular macromolecule is it MOST likely to damage?

options.A: Superoxide (O2•−) damages DNA by causing 8-oxoguanine formation
options.B: Hydroxyl radical (OH•) — the most reactive ROS — causes DNA strand breaks, lipid peroxidation, and protein carbonylation
options.C: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) directly alkylates DNA bases
options.D: Singlet oxygen (1O2) produced by Fe2+ causes lipid peroxidation exclusively

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — Hydroxyl radical (OH•). The Fenton reaction: Fe2+ + H2O2 → Fe3+ + OH• + OH−. The hydroxyl radical is the most reactive and destructive ROS. It causes: DNA damage: strand breaks, oxidative base modification (8-oxoguanine from guanine — if not repaired, leads to G:C→T:A transversions; key in carcinogenesis). Lipid peroxidation: chain reaction damaging membrane phospholipids. Protein carbonylation: oxidizes amino acid side chains. In hereditary hemochromatosis, excess free iron (not bound to ferritin or transferrin) catalyzes Fenton chemistry → chronic oxidative stress → hepatocellular carcinoma, cardiac damage. Option A: Superoxide (O2•−) can cause 8-oxoguanine but INDIRECTLY (through H2O2 and then Fenton reaction). It is not the Fenton product. Option C: H2O2 is a relatively mild oxidant; it doesn't directly alkylate DNA but generates OH• via Fenton. Option D: Singlet oxygen is generated by photosensitization reactions (porphyrins, certain drugs); not by Fe2+. Exam pearl: Antioxidant hierarchy: SOD (O2•− → H2O2) → Catalase or Glutathione peroxidase (H2O2 → H2O). Iron overload + oxidative stress → hemochromatosis complications: cirrhosis, HCC, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, arthritis, bronzing of skin (5 Cs: Cirrhosis, Cardiomyopathy, Chondrocalcinosis, Cortisol/endocrine dysfunction, Carcinoma).

questions.question_text: A 6-year-old boy is admitted with confusion, vomiting, and seizures. Serum ammonia is 680 µmol/L. Plasma amino acid analysis shows elevated glutamine and alanine, and low citrulline. Urine orotic acid is significantly elevated. His 3-year-old brother had died with similar symptoms. Chromosomal analysis is normal (46,XY). Genetic testing reveals a hemizygous mutation. Which condition does this MOST likely represent, and why is urine orotic acid elevated?

options.A: CPS-I deficiency; excess carbamoyl phosphate is converted to orotic acid via the pyrimidine synthesis pathway
options.B: OTC deficiency; excess carbamoyl phosphate (which cannot be used for citrulline synthesis) overflows into the pyrimidine pathway → orotic acid is produced and excreted in urine
options.C: Arginase deficiency; elevated arginine is converted to orotic acid by arginase overflow products
options.D: NAGS deficiency; N-acetylglutamate accumulation activates the pyrimidine synthesis pathway

questions.explanation: Correct answer: B — OTC (Ornithine transcarbamylase) deficiency, the most common urea cycle disorder. OTC is X-linked recessive: (1) Hemizygous males are severely affected (presentation as described). (2) Carrier females may be mildly affected or asymptomatic. OTC catalyzes: Ornithine + Carbamoyl phosphate → Citrulline (in mitochondria). Without OTC: Carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in mitochondria → leaks into cytoplasm → enters pyrimidine synthesis pathway (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, aspartate transcarbamylase pathway) → forms orotic acid (excreted in urine because the full pyrimidine synthesis is overwhelmed). Hence: hyperammonemia + elevated orotic acid + LOW citrulline (OTC deficiency, citrulline cannot be formed). Option A: CPS-I deficiency — carbamoyl phosphate CANNOT be formed → orotic acid is NORMAL or LOW (no substrate for pyrimidine pathway). Option C: Arginase deficiency causes elevated arginine and argininemia; orotic acid is not significantly elevated; presents differently (spastic diplegia, not neonatal coma). Option D: NAGS deficiency → low CPS-I activity → low orotic acid, similar to CPS-I deficiency. Exam pearl: OTC deficiency key features: X-linked (most common urea cycle disorder), elevated orotic acid, low citrulline, hyperammonemia. Treatment: protein restriction, arginine supplementation (to drive urea cycle distally), nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate), liver transplantation.
